purpose:
The decision to fund a local Swap to Stop
scheme has been taken as smoking rates are higher in specific
places and populations, so it is most effectively addressed through
targeted, place- based action rather than a national,
one-size-fits-all approach. Traditional stop smoking services also
don’t reach the whole smoking population, so Swap to Stop
provides an alternative offer that could reach some smokers who
will never engage with the traditional service.
Vaping is a NICE recommended, highly effective tool to quit
smoking. Data from 2024 showed that vapes had been the most popular
aid to quitting among those who had successfully stopped smoking in
the previous 5 years. It is also substantially less harmful than
smoking so can help prevent future hospital admissions and the
development of long-term conditions, compared to if a person
continued smoking. If more people are quitting smoking by using
vapes, it will support the ambition to reduce smoking prevalence in
Doncaster.
The decision to procure access to the Unite platform has been taken
as all the services can access it to purchase vapes from their
preferred brand. It has a wide range of vape products available and
offers competitive pricing. Thereby allowing value for money and
contingency options if a particular product is out of
stock.

decision_maker: Executive Director Policy, Partnership and Investment
purpose:
The Environmental Sustainability team and
Public Health have worked in collaboration to deliver the
affordable warmth program for the last 12 years. Cold, damp homes
have a negative impact on health and wellbeing and lead to an
increased use of our health and care resources. Affordable warmth
is a key preventative factor for promoting health amongst our most
vulnerable communities; a warm, safe home can help maintain
independence and avoid unnecessary reliance on health and social
care services.

It has long been understood that certain people, such as the very
young, the oldest and people with long-term disability or illness,
are particularly at risk of poor health from cold homes (BEIS,
2015). In addition to the health impacts of a cold home, fuel
poverty affects the financial wellbeing of households and reduces
available income, thus impacting on wider health and wellbeing. In
Doncaster it is estimated that 22,349 (16.1%) households are in
fuel poverty, 2023.

The Affordable Warmth service will:

Provide fuel poor and vulnerable private sector owner occupied
households with grant funding to repair/replace boilers and/or
heating systems and other energy measures. This includes but is not
limited to Boiler on Prescription intervention. Community members
will be identified as most at risk due to health conditions that
are exacerbated by a cold home. Implement the energy measures
required, this can range from low level measures such as draft
insulation to full heating systems, radiators, pumps, control
systems or other ancillary materials.


Be a single point of contact for stakeholders referring
householders and assess eligibility for the scheme.

Provide behavioural advice to manage energy effectively and secure
the most appropriate fuel tariff and billing system.

Be committed to providing a safe, sensitive, non-judgemental and
non-oppressive support service.

Provide energy saving tips for the home, including getting the most
out of your heating and hot water system.

Access energy efficiency grants, including grants that will
complement the BOP fund.

Facilitate or attend a number of Community Events to provide
information, advice, guidance on winter warmth services available,
with relevant activities available to engage the target
audience.

Order, distribution and manage winter warmth items for those at
risk when appropriate.

Deliver training to health and wider professionals, this will be
undertaken by the Home Energy Officer via team meetings with wider
local organisations and partners. The training outcomes will be to
gain an understanding of Excess Winter Deaths within the Borough
and an understanding of the term “Fuel Poverty”, to
understand and refer to BOP and other support and the impact on a
person’s health.

Offer training to health and social care staff as part of the
‘Preparing for Winter’ communication plan in order to
raise their awareness and understanding of the risks associated
with a cold home and what they can do to ensure vulnerable people
keep warm. Information relating to the risks to vulnerable people
and simple messages will be given to frontline staff as part of
self-management advice.

purpose:
Public footpath No.21 Fishlake commences near Jubilee Bridge and
runs in a south, south-westerly direction alongside the River Don
to Fishlake where it then continues to its junction with Fishlake
Nab.

The definitive alignment of the path cannot be walked in its
entirety. The legal line follows the old course of the river. Both
the path and the old alignment are clearly shown on the draft and
provisional maps produced during the original definitive mapping
process; however, the definitive map shows a different alignment of
the
river. It is not known when the river was realigned, but the path
shown on the definitive map still follows the old alignment. The
result is the legal line of the path crosses the river twice,
without any provision to cross at either location.

Other longstanding obstructions exist along the path. The
definitive line is obstructed where it meets Fishlake Nab by a
concrete wall, which forms part of the flood defence. The path on
the ground starts slightly further towards Fishlake. It is also
obstructed by flood arches.

There will be no costs incurred in physically providing the
footpath as the route already exists and any future maintenance
costs will be funded from the Public Right of Way budget, as is the
case with the path currently.

The local ward members, the cabinet member for Environment Housing
and Safer Communities, Fishlake Parish Council, both Stainforth and
Thorne and Moorends
Town Councils’, the Planning Policy and Environment Team and
representatives from local prescribed organisations and statutory
undertakers were sent details of the proposal.

No objections were received and the comments that were made were
supportive of the proposal.

Due regard considerations - Of the protected characteristic groups,
disability, age and pregnancy and maternity are the most relevant
in the context of this proposed footpath diversion. Any alteration
to the rights of way network has the potential to
cause problems for all users, but users with disabilities, the less
mobile or who are pregnant may be disadvantaged more so. An initial
due regard assessment has been carried out on the proposal,
reference PL-I-00037. The initial assessment
determined that no further action is needed.

Further info provided on ODR.

purpose:
The Council has received confirmation of its
Homelessness Prevention, Rough Sleeping and Domestic
Abuse Grant allocation for 2026/27. The funding is included within
the approved budget but has increased
so the purpose of this decision is to approve the proposed
allocation of resources in line with grant
conditions, statutory duties and local priorities.
St Leger Homes delivers the statutory homelessness service on
behalf of the Council. This includes
homelessness prevention, housing advice and assistance,
homelessness assessments, temporary
accommodation management, tenancy sustainment, private rented
sector access, move-on
accommodation and wider prevention activity.
Adult Social Care deliver a range of services relating to the care,
support and accommodation of people
experiencing rough sleeping and multiple disadvantage. These
services support individuals experiencing
long-term rough sleeping, trauma, mental ill-health, substance
misuse and wider social exclusion.
Domestic abuse services also provide support to individuals and
families at risk of homelessness due to
unsafe accommodation, helping victims access safe housing and
specialist support.
The Government has introduced significant changes to homelessness
and rough sleeping funding through
the Fair Funding Review. Separate homelessness and rough sleeping
grants have now been consolidated
into a single Homelessness Prevention, Rough Sleeping and Domestic
Abuse Grant. The revised
arrangements place greater emphasis on:
• prevention and early intervention
• reducing rough sleeping
• partnership and whole-system working
• flexibility of local delivery
• improved outcomes for vulnerable residents
The grant supports local authorities to discharge their statutory
duties under the Housing Act 1996 and
deliver against local homelessness strategies and national
homelessness objectives.

purpose:
The Council has been awarded funding through
the Government’s Long-Term Rough Sleeping
Innovation Programme, which forms part of the national strategy to
reduce and ultimately end
long-term rough sleeping.
The programme places significant emphasis on partnership working,
system leadership and the
development of integrated responses to long-term rough sleeping.
Local authorities are
expected to demonstrate:
• Earlier identification and prevention
• More personalised and flexible responses
• Stronger integration across services and partners
• Improved governance and collective accountability
• Clear evidence of improved outcomes and system change
The programme specifically requires local authorities to develop
stronger whole-system
approaches to long-term rough sleeping, including coordinated
governance, shared priorities,
partnership-led delivery and integrated responses across
agencies.
• Driving innovation and service development where existing
pathways are not meeting
need
The role will operate across organisational boundaries and support
the development of a
sustainable partnership model for homelessness prevention and rough
sleeping, including
At present, responsibility for homelessness and rough sleeping

voluntary, community and faith
sector. Whilst significant work is already undertaken across the

responses for individuals

The proposed Homelessness Coordinator / Strategic Lead role will

• Providing oversight and alignment of homelessness prevention
and rough sleeping

• Coordinating multiple interdependent workstreams, including

accommodation, support and move-on pathways
• Supporting collective prioritisation, decision-making and
governance arrangements
• Improving coordination between operational services and
strategic partners
• Supporting the development of shared approaches to case
management, information
sharing and performance monitoring
• Ensuring local approaches remain aligned with national
policy, funding requirements
and programme expectations
governance arrangements, shared accountability, pathway development
and multi-agency
problem solving.
Alongside this, funding will support the development of innovative
and flexible pathways for
individuals experiencing long-term rough sleeping who are unable to
engage with, or sustain,
traditional accommodation offers. This cohort often experiences
multiple disadvantage, trauma,
poor physical and mental health, substance misuse and repeat
homelessness, resulting in
continued use of emergency and crisis services.

purpose:
City of Doncaster Council (CDC) is seeking to
procure a compliant and cost-effective solution for the placement
of statutory public notices, primarily within the printed press,
ensuring legal compliance, transparency, and public
accessibility.
As an Authority, CDC is required to carry out a range of statutory
functions under various legislation, including the Traffic
Management Act 2004, Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984, Highways Act
1980, Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, and the Town and Country
Planning Act 1990, amongst others. This legislation requires
certain notices to be made publicly available via the printed
press. While these are typically published in local newspapers, in
some instances publication in national press is also
required.
CDC currently produces approximately 1,200 notices per year that
require press advertising.
Without a suitable contract in place, CDC would be at risk of
failing to meet its statutory obligations to provide public
notice.

protect the Council

recognise the structural realities mean that fuel prices are likely
to rise further, a
pragmatic assessment of the situation would indicate the providers
cost base is

purpose:
The statutory gambling levy represents a
generational change to funding
arrangements and a significant transformation in the
government’s commitment to
strengthening efforts to understand, tackle and treat
gambling-related harm.

Operators are required to pay into the levy by October each year.
The levy is collected and administered by the Gambling Commission
under the strategic direction of the UK government, and has
replaced the previous system of voluntary industry contributions.
Levy funding will be directed in specific proportions for the
purposes of research, prevention and treatment.

The priority for the government is to increase the level of
investment and strengthen the provision of projects and services to
understand, tackle and treat gambling-related harm in order to
improve outcomes for the public.
The funds are split into 3 elements; 20% for Research, 50% for
Treatment and 30% for Prevention.

The Dept of Health and Social Care hold the funds and will
distribute to Directors of Public Health via the Office for Health
Improvement and Disparities. This is the first time that funds have
been made available to Public Health to explore and
seek how to prevent gambling harms in LA areas.

The Levy will initially be distributed in this way for 2 financial
years, 2026/27 and 2027/28 and will be paid quarterly. The amount
allocated to Doncaster Public Health for 2026/27 is
£78512.71. The 2027/28 allocation is expected to be of
the
same value.

purpose:
The City of Doncaster Council (CDC), as the
statutory Highway Authority, has a legal responsibility to ensure
that the public highway remains safe for all users under the
Highways Act 1980. When sections of the network become flooded, CDC
is required to intervene to prevent significant risks to motorists
and pedestrians, including vehicle loss, collisions, and
individuals becoming stranded. In recent years, during multiple
heavy rainfall events, CDC has repeatedly deployed operational
teams to temporarily close affected roads and station a jetting
tanker on site for extended periods to remove surface water. This
reactive arrangement has been essential to maintain public safety,
but it places considerable strain on limited resources.
The repeated deployment of tankers to a single high-risk location
represents an inefficient use of a critical asset, particularly
during severe weather when the Council must meet its statutory
duties under the Flood and Water Management Act 2010. With only a
small fleet of tankers available, dedicating one unit for an entire
day restricts the authority’s ability to manage other
drainage emergencies or deliver urgent flood-risk mitigation across
the wider network. This conflicts with the requirement for local
authorities to take a risk-based, proportionate, and resilient
approach to flood event response and infrastructure
management.

purpose:
Towards the end of February 2021, OFSTED
received a whistle blow referral which was reported to the
Doncaster Children’s Services Trust. The DCS and safeguarding
partners took decisive action to protect the residents at that
time.
2. The Doncaster Safeguarding Partnership Executives took a
decision at the beginning of March 2021 to initiate a Complex Abuse
Inquiry.
3. Extraordinary funding has been agreed by Cabinet and the
Children Safeguarding partnership for years 2021/2022, 2023/24,
2024/25 and 2025/26 to fund the social care element of the
investigation. South Yorkshire Police is resourcing the policing
element of the investigation.
4. To date a team of social workers have undertaken the building of
life story packs, recovery planning and the completion of Local
Authority Designated Officer investigations. The management of the
team has been dealing with strategic oversight, partner engagement,
including the Disclosure and Barring Service and regulators. This
was funded through the key decisions taken by Cabinet.
5. The operation continues to evolve into a multi-layered and
legally complex landscape. A growing number of Subject Access
Requests (SARs) have been received and in addition to large numbers
of Freedom Of Information (FOI) requests. Substantiated allegation
management meetings as part of the LADO function, led to Disclosure
and Barring Service (DBS) referrals, with subsequent reviews and
information sharing commencing on an individual basis, between the
social work and DBS team. Safer Recruitment enquiries for
individual staff and Regulatory enquiries continue to also be
received. This will continue, due to residual risk in the
system.
6. The inquiry is entering its final stage. Social work expertise
in terms of building life story packs have now concluded. The work
that remains are focussing on dealing redacting and sharing of
information with local authority areas, their safeguarding partners
and families. The disclosure of information requests is dealt with
in the relevant legal frameworks through Subject Access requests,
Freedom of Information requests, supporting the Disclosure and
Barring Service in their investigation, Regulatory support and the
Police investigation itself.
7. An operational end of investigation report is expected by June
2026. A strategic evaluation programme of work, concluding in a
report will also be lead and completed by the external scrutineer
of the investigation.
8. It is therefore proposed that from April 2026, the social work
leadership capacity and two business support roles continue to
support the investigation for up to six months to the value
of £176,870. In additional to this there may also be external
legal costs incurred, which are currently difficult to quantify and
will require appropriate funding.
9. It is anticipated that the remainder of the operational delivery
of the investigation will conclude within the first 3 months of
2026/27, and it will take 2 – 3 months to transfer all
remaining functions, as set out above, to the Council. Therefore,
the request for funding is for up to 6
months unless there is a significant change in the direction of
travel for the enquiry.

decision_maker: Assistant Director of Children, Young People and Families
purpose:
To continue the DAS service offer.
DAS has been an essential pillar of support for the Doncaster
community since its inception in April 2022. It was established to
fill a critical gap in post-diagnostic support, ensuring that
families not only receive guidance after a diagnosis but also gain
the confidence and knowledge needed to support their child
throughout the assessment journey.
Workshops delivered by DAS offer more than information, they create
empowerment. These interactive sessions help individuals deepen
their understanding of autism, feel supported, and develop
practical strategies to overcome challenges. Importantly, the group
setting fosters a sense of belonging and connection, enabling
families and individuals to share experiences and build supportive
networks.
The one-to-one post-diagnostic offer provides highly personalised
support. This service helps individuals process and reflect on
their diagnosis, understand what it means for them, and develop
confidence in sharing this understanding with others. Such tailored
support is vital for emotional well-being and self-advocacy.
No other service in Doncaster currently offers this level of
specialist, community-focused provision. The DAS team has spent
three years developing unique expertise, combining strong community
links through Doncaster Parent Voice (DPV) with educational insight
via partnerships with the Educational Psychology Service and
ASCETS. This dual perspective ensures that DAS delivers a truly
holistic and bespoke service that cannot be replicated within
existing local capacity or working practices.
In short, DAS is not just a service-it is a lifeline for families
and individuals navigating autism.

purpose:
The various wastes collected by the Council as
part of its day-to-day activities are collectively
termed “Local Authority Collected Waste” (formerly
known as Municipal Waste).

The Council has a duty to collect and / or dispose of Local
Authority Collected Waste
[‘Controlled Waste(s)’] pursuant to:
a) Section 45 (1) of the Environmental Protection Act 1990;
b) Section 51 (1) of the Environmental Protection Act 1990;
c) Section 89 (1) (2) of the Environmental Protection Act
1990;
and other relevant legislation that requires the Council to remove
items deposited on land such
as the Highways Act 1980 (excluding liquid wastes).

The Council has various re-use, recycling and recovery contracts
in-place for managing Local
Authority Collected Waste.

The Council entered into a four [4] year Contract [with AWM] for
the disposal of ‘Municipal
Waste’ on 5th April 2020. This Contract provides an outlet
for the proportion of Local Authority
Collected Waste that remained unsuitable for existing re-use,
recycling and / or recovery
contracts due to their composition, size or weight. For
example:
a) Bulky Waste Items that exceed 25kg in weight.
b) Bulky Waste items that will not fit into a standard receptacle
for Household Waste.
c) Mixed Municipal waste from fly-tipping.

The Contract with AWM is due to expire on 4th April 2026.

Procurement Regulations and Financial Procedure Rules required the
Council to undertake a
new procurement exercise for the above Contract to ensure
continuation of service delivery after
the expiry date.

The Council has now conducted a procurement exercise in compliance
with Public Procurement
Regulations in accordance with decision ref: PLACE25
0123.

The
Mayor and Cabinet approve the admission arrangements for the
2027/2028 Academic Year as detailed in the report:-

 
·      
Community School Admission Arrangements
·      
Community School Nursery Admission Arrangements
·      
Primary Co-ordinated Admission Arrangements

Secondary Co-ordinated Admission Arrangements

 Councillor Sue
Farmer, Cabinet Member for Equalities, Education and Skills
introduced a report, which set out the requirements for the
adoption of schemes for co-ordinating the Admission Arrangements
for Primary and Secondary Schools and sought Cabinet’s
approval of the Admission Arrangements for the City of
Doncaster’s Schools for the 2027/2028 School Year.
 
The co-ordinated admission arrangements to
schools is a
statutory responsibility of the Council and must be determined
annually and sets out to provide an equal opportunity for all
parents to apply for school places at the same time through a
process co-ordinated by the Council.
 
Applications for all stages of entry continue
to be made
available via the Council’s website, with a paper application
also available, but there continued to be a high percentage made
online. The effectiveness of the current arrangements was reflected in the
consistently high rates of pupil preferences being met, with 98% of
secondary age pupils and 99% of primary age pupils being offered
one of their choices.

The options considered were set out in detail
in paragraphs 23 to 37 of the report.

Cabinet:-
 

1)   
Approve the City of Doncaster Council’s Tax
Base for the 2026/2027 year as 89,231 band D equivalent
dwellings as detailed at Appendix 1 attached to the report;
and
 

2)   
Approve the City of Doncaster Council’s Tax
Base for the 2026/2027 year for each part of its area at parish
level as detailed in Appendix 2 attached to the
report.
 

Ros Jones, Mayor of Doncaster and Portfolio
Holder for Budget, Policy and Economic Development introduced a
report, which sought Cabinet’s approval of the calculation of
the proposed Council Tax Base for Doncaster for the 2026/27
financial year, as detailed in Appendix 1 of the report.
 
The Local Authorities (Calculation of Council
Tax Base) (England) Regulations 2012 make arrangements for the
setting of the Council Tax. These arrangements include the
determination of the Council Tax Base and the regulations prescribe
how this calculation should be carried out
 
The City of Doncaster Council was statutorily
required under the Local Authorities (Calculation of Council Tax
Base) (England) Regulations 2012 to determine the level of Council
Tax base for individual properties for 2026/27. It represented the
number of properties that will be subject to Council Tax, and which
are expressed in terms of their Band D equivalents using a
prescribed formula after allowing for the effect of exemptions,
discounts, premiums and reliefs.
 
The agreed Tax Base for the City of Doncaster
Council for 2026/27 will be used in the 2026/27 Budget and Council
Tax setting calculation. The Tax Base is also used by the major
precepting bodies (South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue and South
Yorkshire Police) and the local parish councils to determine their
precept requirements and must be set before the end of January in
order to meet their requirements.
 
The proposed Council Tax Base for the City of
Doncaster for 2026/2027 is 89,231 band D equivalent
dwellings. This represents an increase of 1,147 band D equivalent
dwellings compared to the current year’s Tax Base of
88,084.
 
A schedule of the proposed Council Tax base
for each Parish/Town Council was set out in Appendix 2 of the
report.

The
Local Authorities (Calculation of Council Tax Base) (England)
Regulations 2012 prescribe how the calculation of the Council Tax
Base must be carried out. There are no other options.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the City of Doncaster Council's Tax Base for the 2026/2027 year.

content:
Cabinet:-
 

1)   
Agree that the draft City Borough Strategy be presented to Full
Council for approval on 22nd January,
2026; and
 

2)   
Note that the City Borough Statement will inform the
Council’s Corporate Plan, with specific actions for 2026/27
identified.

Mayor Ros Jones presented a report to Cabinet
that outlined the refresh of the Borough Strategy (Doncaster
Delivering Together) prior to its progression to Full Council for
approval.
 
 
 Team Doncaster’s borough strategy
is included in the Council’s Constitution as a statutory
plan. All strategies, including this refresh, must be adopted by
Full Council. As part of the formal approval process through to
Full Council, engagement has taken place with the council’s
Overview and Scrutiny Management Committee (OSMC).
 
The principal mission of Doncaster Delivering
Together is to have thriving people, places and planet, balancing
the wellbeing of all these to create the kind of borough we want in
the future. Bringing this to reality continues to be a shared
responsibility between public agencies, businesses, residents and
the voluntary, community and faith sector. The DDT refresh will set
out the key actions that will be Team Doncaster’s focus up to
2030.
 
Much has been achieved since DDT was launched
and the refresh will continue to build on this progress with a
summary of achievements provided below.
 
·      Doncaster
has attracted £1.2 billion in investment since 2020, and the
reopening of Doncaster Sheffield Airport will transform
connectivity and create a sustainable aviation hub.
·     The
restoration of the Corn Exchange has
transformed cultural infrastructure.
·       Major
events such as Rugby League World Cup, Railway 200 Exhibition,
Pride and the Balloon Festival have attracted tens of thousands of
visitors.
·      Get
Doncaster Moving initiatives have helped more people to become
physically active.
·       Creative health and learning
are improving wellbeing and inclusion.
·      Holiday
activity programmes provided over 37,000 places for local children
during summer 2025.
·      Family Hubs
and Early Help services are supporting more children and
families. 
·      More
5-year-olds now have a good level of development, above national
average, along with attainment at Key Stage 2. 
·      More
than 7,500 energy efficiency measures have been delivered to homes
and over 9,000 properties have been fitted with solar
panels.
·      Nearly
410,000 trees have been planted under the One Million Tree
Challenge.
 
Despite this progress, it was noted that key
challenges remain. Child poverty and deprivation remained high,
crime and ASB rates exceed regional averages and air quality has
worsened slightly. Recycling rates have stagnated and skills gaps
persist, particularly in Level 3 attainment and
apprenticeships. 
 
Locally, this refresh coincides with a new
administrative term. This administrative term would run
concurrently with the second half of DDT and would allow a refocus
on the things that mean the most to those living and working in
Doncaster and would look to build on the progress made, capitalise
on recent opportunities and react to new challenges.
 

The options considered were:
 

1)   
Not refresh the DDT Borough Strategy and Delivery Programme;
and
 

2)   
Refresh the DDT Borough Strategy and Delivery Programme
(Recommended Option)
topline: The Doncaster Council has decided to refresh the Borough Strategy to create a thriving borough for the future, with specific actions identified for 2026/27.

Cabinet Agree:-
 
1)   
To approve a three-year property asset
disposal plan as detailed in this report and including the sites
and properties listed in Appendix 1. (as part of a managed
three-year disposal programme, to support the Council's Capital
Programme.
 




2)   
for delegated authority to be given to
the Property Officer in consultation with the Portfolio Holder for
Environment, Housing and Safer Communities and the Chief Financial
Officer to approve the terms of disposal for any sales exceeding
£1 million within the Disposal Programme, subject to
obtaining appropriate financial and legal advice and ensuring that
the disposal achieves no less than best consideration.
 
3)   
Any additions or further changes to the
programme will be made in accordance with the Council’s
agreed Governance arrangements.




 





Councillor Glyn Jones, Cabinet Member for
Environment, Housing and Safer Communities, presented a report that
outlined the Councils intention to implement a three-year programme
of asset disposals on sites across the borough. The release of
surplus assets for disposal will encourage new development,
creating housing, jobs and growth in the local economy and is
essential in providing vital capital funding to enable the delivery
of the Councils Capital Programme.
 




Cabinet
were
asked to consider the asset disposal programme proposals contained
within the report and confirm their support for a three-year
managed programme to support the Councils Capital Programme. The
Council's Capital Programme was partially funded through proceeds
generated from the sale or disposal of property assets owned by the
Council and the report noted that the creation of a
programme
of planned
property disposals would generate capital receipts that would be
used in line with the Capital Strategy




 
A list of
assets proposed for disposal was contained within Appendix 1
to the report. Approval for sale will still allow other options for
use of each asset, to align with the Councils ongoing strategic
objectives during the period of this three-year
programme.
 

Members
noted that it was important to note that prior to marketing for
sale, each

asset would
be subject to a consultation exercise, in common with all sales
of

Council
assets and in accordance with the Council’s disposal policy.
Each asset

review also
considers Legal and Planning restrictions on a possible sale, with
consultation also undertaken with Ward Members. 




 
 




 






Do
Nothing

Without a managed programme of asset disposals, funding will not be
available to support Capital Programme
activities.

 





Deliver a managed programme of
disposals of Council property assets over a 3-year
period.

(Recommended option) A planned approach will
increase certainty in decision making in the Capital Programme. In the absence of asset disposals to
fund its initiatives, the Capital Programme will lack the necessary support from
generated capital receipts.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a three-year property asset disposal plan to support the Council's Capital Programme.

content:
Cabinet approve Your Care and Support:
Doncaster’s Adult Social Care Local Account 2026.

While not
mandatory, there was a national expectation that all Councils with
Adult Social Services responsibilities publish an annual local
account which reviews the previous year’s performance and
describes priorities for the next year. With this in mind,
Councillor David Nevett presented Doncaster’s local account
for 2026, entitled “Your Care and Support” which had
been put together alongside people with lived experience of care
and support in Doncaster under the auspices of the ‘Making it
Real’ Board which was a mix of adults with lived experience
of care, as well as representatives from Adults, Wellbeing and
Culture.
Your Care and
Support” showcases what is good in terms of care and
support in Doncaster as well as reflecting on areas that required
further development, drawing on both comparative data and
first-hand testimony from Doncaster people who have experience of
care and support. It includes the priorities that Making it Real
Board members have identified for Adult Social Care in 2026 and the
key actions that were
required to deliver these.
“Your Care
and Support” is now
co-produced on an annual basis with each version
improving as we further expand our approach to coproduction and to
gathering feedback. The 2026 version further develops the ambition
and progress that was set out in the 2025 document.
This would look to
ensure that improvements to Adult Social Care would include the
following:-
-      Increased satisfaction and better lives for Doncaster
people.
-      Increased satisfaction and morale for Doncaster’s Adult
Social Care workforce.
-      More
sustainable use of resources by preventing, reducing and delaying people losing independence
and wellbeing.
Following the
presentation of the report, Councillor David Nevett invited Helen
Stirland, Co-chair of
Doncaster’s Making It Real Board, to present her lived
experiences as users of Doncaster’s Adult Care Services.
Helen praised the Council’s approach to
“co-production” and emphasised the good work that had been
done. Helen commented that she enjoyed working alongside the
Council and the support she had received as a result had enabled
her to live independently at home.
Members thanked the Service Users for
attending and reiterated how important it was to work together. The
input that they gave was valuable and provided information on a
range of issues. The Mayor concluded the discussions by conveying her
thanks to carers all across Doncaster who supported and enabled
many individuals to carry on living independently in their
homes.

Option
1
Not
producing a Local Account;
Option
2
Council
officers compiling a Local Account;
Option 3
 
Council
officers compiling a Local Account alongside Doncaster people with
lived experience of care and support as part of an ongoing
programme of improvement (Recommended Option).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve Doncaster's Adult Social Care Local Account 2026, focusing on improving care and support services in the region.

content:
Cabinet approve Doncaster’s
Carers’ Journey 2026

Carers are people
who support a partner, family member, friend or neighbour who
relies on this support to help them live their life. There is a
large amount of evidence both nationally and internationally about
the essential nature of the support that unpaid carers provide, and
how statutory services like those provided by the Council and the
NHS would be overwhelmed if it did not exist.
Doncaster’s
Carers Journey 2026 has been co-produced by Council officers and
Team Doncaster partners alongside unpaid carers and is designed to
review what has been done to better support unpaid carers in 2025,
and what is planned to be achieved over 2026.
Doncaster’s Carers Journey 2026 is
structured around six themes which were chosen by Doncaster carers
themselves:

-       Identification

-       Recognition

-       Information and Advice

-       Rights

-       Connection

-       Independence and Wellbeing
 
The document also
sets out ways for more of Doncaster’s carers of all ages to
have their voices heard as it was essential to keep track of
improvements to the identification, recognition, information,
advice, rights, connection and wellbeing that Doncaster’s
carers should be experiencing from the Council and Team Doncaster
partners
Following the presentation of the
report, Councillor David Nevett invited Debbie Osborne,
The Co-Chair of the Carers
Strategic Oversight Board and Carers Action Group,
to present her lived experience as a user of
Doncaster’s Adult Care Services. Debbie praised the
Council’s approach to “co-production” and the
value of asking individuals what assistance they need from the
Council and commented she hoped the work done to support carers in
Children’s services would be mirrored in Adults moving forward. A lot of improvements had
been made, but there was still work to do.
 
Cabinet thanked Debbie for attending and
sharing her lived experiences as it provided valuable feedback and
insight into the work carried out. Members paid tribute to the work
of people on all sides undertaken to provide residents with
valuable help and support to live their lives independently.
 
 


Option 1

 

Not producing a “Doncaster’s Carers
Journey 2026.

 

Option 2

Team Doncaster officers compiling the
document.
 

Option 3

Team Doncaster officers compiling the document
alongside Doncaster carers as part of an ongoing programme of
improvement (recommended option)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve Doncaster's Carers Journey 2026, aimed at better supporting unpaid carers in the region.

provides a framework for the next phase of development, setting out
a new vision for the city centre and the key activity which will
underpin delivery. This strategy identifies the Waterdale as a strategically important site
for redevelopment.
 
There is and has been, significant investment
in regenerating the Civic and Cultural Quarter and the City Gateway
area at the rail station. These areas are positioned at opposite
sides of the city centre and so it is now important to focus on the
corridor between these regenerating areas. The Waterdale and adjacent Colonnades areas are
under performing and characterised by derelict land and vacant
units. Progressing a regeneration scheme for these areas would
effectively join up the city from a regeneration perspective
significantly enhancing the look feel and vibrancy of the city.
 
Once procurement has taken place, detailed
master planning work will take place by the developer in liaison
with CDC and in line with its vision for the city centre. Work will
progress through a number of ‘Gateways’ in the process
which provide the opportunity to take stock and assess whether to
proceed to the next gateway or halt the project. This would help
control and limit the exposure to financial risks.
 
Councillor James Church commended the report,
which outlined a fantastic opportunity for the City. It was vital
that the City was regenerated in order to boost the economy and
support the residents and businesses of Doncaster.


OPTION 1

Support the recommendations contained within this
report to progress the necessary works to regenerate the
Waterdale and Colonnades areas.
(Recommended Option)

 

OPTION 2

Reject the recommendations contained within this
report to progress the necessary works to regenerate the
Waterdale and Colonnades
areas.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to authorize the procurement of a developer to deliver a regeneration scheme for Waterdale and Colonnades in Doncaster.

content:
Cabinet Agree to:-

 

1)   
approve the allocation of grant funding to the
specific projects, as updated and outlined in this report, in
accordance with the LUF 3 MOU and approve the addition of these
schemes to the Council’s capital programme; and
 





2)   
provide delegated authority to the Executive
Director of Place, the Executive Director of Corporate Resources
and Chief Financial Officer in consultation with the Mayor, to
deliver the proposals outlined within the report and summarised
below:

 

·      
Enter into agreement with Harmby to sub-lease the
refurbished retail units and make the necessary investment to allow
Market traders to occupancy these units.

·      
Repurpose the Market Hall for a commercial or
community use.

·      
Demolish the multi-story carpark and create a
surface carpark.





 




 

 




The Deputy Mayor, Councillor Glyn Jones,
presented a report detailing proposals for retail units, Mexborough
Market and the Multi Storey Car Park in Mexborough.

 

Mexborough was undergoing substantial investment in a range of
regeneration schemes.  The LUF3 funded elements of the
Mexborough High Street works which started in August 2025 with an
estimated contract duration of approximately 21 months and
includes:

 

·       High
Street landscape scheme

·       Bank
Street improvements

·       Improved access to the Athletic Sports Club

·       Swinton Road improvements

·       Station Road improvements

·       Shop
front improvement scheme

 

The report considered by Cabinet sought to update the Cabinet
Report dated 31st March 2025 which
provided approval to accept up to £17,950,341 of Levelling Up
Fund (LUF) Round 3 money awarded to Doncaster Council by the
Department of Levelling Up, Housing and Communities (DLUHC) (now
Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government
(MHCLG)).  This included the outlined
proposals for Retail
Units, Mexborough Market and Multistory Car Park (MSCP).

 





There was an approved allocated
£1.78 million from LUF3 funding to implement improvements to
address the issues identified within the report in order to enhance
the public offer within Mexborough, make it more commercially
viable and reduce the asset maintenance liability for
CDC.

 





The report sought approval to address
those concerns identified in the masterplan and community
engagement by leasing and refurbishing the retail units in York
Square,to offer an incentive to repurpose the existing Market Hall
& demolish the Multistorey Carpark.





 
Delivery of these
programmes would provide a range of benefits for the residents of
Mexborough, primarily improving the retail experience, providing
additional accessibility to the Market Hall and by expanding the
retail offer into York Square.  Providing a greater markets
experience would look to support the high street and the early
evening economy whilst it would also address concerns raised over the blight and
anti-social activity at the Multistorey Carpark.
 




Members noted that the capital
investment currently available for Mexborough was unprecedented and
unlikely to be available again. It is imperative that the core
issues in Mexborough are targeted and
the funding utilised by this opportunity.




Accepting the funding would allow
Doncaster to deliver reactive improvements to the Market, focusing
on improving the heart of Mexborough’s retail core and would
allow the delivery of positive changes to a failing town
centre.
 
Members welcomed the report as the level of
improvements it would bring about was unprecedented. Mayor Jones
paid thanks to Mexborough Ward Councillors both past and present
who had supported the scheme and looked forward to seeing the
regeneration of the area take place.




 




 





Option A - Do
something- Proposal:

1.   
Lease on the 9 units in York Square

-      
Refurbish the retail units in York Square

-      
Offer these units up to the existing market traders
into York Square units

 

2.   
Offer incentive to redevelop the market Hall to
repurposing to be more

commercially viable

 

3.   
Demolish the Multi Story Car Park

-      
Install new surface carpark

-      
Make good and improve exposed walls

 




Option B - Do nothing- Continue to see
the decline of the 800 year old
market.  Continuation of ongoing
substantial and significant maintenance and liability
costs.  The continued decline in
footfall challenging the viability of the Market.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve grant funding for projects in Mexborough, including refurbishing retail units, repurposing the Market Hall, and demolishing the Multi Storey Car Park.

purpose:
The council has utilised the Peoplesafe lone
worker system for the past four years, with adoption across a wide
range of services and over 1,000 active users. This system provides
a robust solution for mitigating risks associated with lone
working, ensuring employee safety during diverse work activities
and reducing potential litigation exposure for the authority.

The Peoplesafe MYSOS solution is available through the G-Cloud 14
Framework which costs £9 a month per unit. Any funding will
be identified by individual Budget Holders through their own
service budgets. Service managers will also ascertain individual
service needs via activity risk assessments. Current spend for a 4
year contract is £164,303 and is expected to continue at this
level.

Our intentions are to procure a 4 year contract through the G-Cloud
14 Framework which has been approved via TGB. A contract can be
procured through G-Cloud 14 for up to 3 years plus a 12 month
extension.

The Deputy Mayor, Councillor Glyn Jones,
presented the Statement of Licensing Policy to the Council for
consideration and approval.
 
It was noted that the Licensing
Act 2003 required that local licensing authorities review and
determine their ‘statement of licensing policy’ every
five years and the policy must address the four licensing
objectives set out in the Act, namely:
 

·        
The
prevention of crime and disorder

·        
Public
safety

·        
The
prevention of public nuisance

·        
The
protection of children from harm
 
Council noted that the revised
policy had been the subject of a statutory consultation which
sought the views of responsible authorities, the licensed trade,
legal representatives, elected members and the wider public. It was
also noted that the revised policy was largely unchanged from the
current version. Details of the changes made before and following
the consultation, were documented within the report.
 
RESOLVED that Council approve the adoption
of the reviewed policy.

purpose:
1. This decision approves the inclusion of the
Council Chamber Microphone System Refresh into the Capital
Programme 2025/26. This will enable the necessary funds to be made
available to replace and install new microphones, voting modules,
and supporting software for the Council and integrate them within
the voting and conference system.

2. The Council Chamber is the main forum for Council decision
making, discussion and debate. It also provides a facility that can
be used for briefings, training and other events for Members and
officers.

3. There is no legal requirement to record, publish or broadcast
Council or committee meetings. However, the public and Members do
need to be able to hear proceedings and there needs to be clarity
over decision-making. There is however, an expectation by the
public that Council meetings are recorded and published and this is
now common practice amongst most Councils. As well as promoting
openness and transparency, it also ensures an
“official” version of a meeting is in the public
domain. The Council Chamber is also used by internal Council
departments, partners and third parties (including Coronial
inquests) and has the potential to generate additional income for
the Council as a meeting space.

n 2013 a cabinet report authorised the
delegated authority to establish Primary Authority Relationships
with Business.
Vertu have expressed a desire to develop a Primary Authority
relationship with this service. They currently have over 200
branches across the UK.
Initially Trading standards will provide for the formal setting up
of the primary authority arrangements through the
Government’s website provision on their register.
The Authority can decide not to participate in any Primary
Authority agreements – This would not support the central
government initiative to support local businesses and the
economy.
The Authority can decide to support appropriate Primary Authority
approaches and enter into agreements with businesses under the
Primary Authority Scheme. This will support the local business,
encourage economic growth and identify Doncaster as a Council that
is keen to support its local economy and Doncaster as a place where
new and relocating businesses can be assured of a supporting
regulatory environment.
